title: Living his calm
hook: detachment here means love without clutching

segments.voice: Yesterday, fifteen ragas, and your line: a raga of his own. Did a song change your mood before its words arrived? This week, the ninth Guru told us: level in all weather, stay in hard times, scent in the flower, this is your work, live in the world, shining. Today, how to live it. Day five hundred eighty-eight.
screen: `FIFTEEN RAGAS — A RAGA OF HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: A parent is teaching a child to ride a bike, running alongside with one hand on the back of the seat. The parent's legs are burning, the child is wobbling, and at some point the hand has to come off, a little at a time. Grip too tight and the child never learns to balance. Let go too soon and they fall. The love is in the loosening. All week, Guru Tegh Bahadur has been saying the world is passing. So does that mean we should love it less? Today the week's hymns add up to an answer.
screen: `RUNNING ALONGSIDE THE BIKE.` → `THE LOVE IS IN THE LOOSENING.` → `SHOULD WE LOVE LESS?`

segments.voice: In Sikh teaching, detachment doesn't mean running away. It's a householder's path. Guru Tegh Bahadur was married to Mata Gujri, and was father to the boy who became Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition remembers long years of quiet meditation at Bakala, and he still lived in a family, traveled, founded the town that became Anandpur, and in the end went to Delhi, where Sikhs remember he gave his life for others. So when his hymns say the world is passing, the point isn't to stop caring. Look at what this week taught. The steady one in Sorath sees gold and dust alike, and merges with the Lord like water into water. The friends who leave in hard times were loving their own comfort. The scent is in the flower, not in the forest. Remembering is the real work, and life without it slips by. Put them together and you get a kind of love that holds without gripping. Guru Nanak gave Sikhs the picture for it: a lotus that grows in water but stays dry, a duck that swims all day and isn't soaked. Those are the images Sikhs reach for when they talk about living in the world without drowning in it. Love without clutching doesn't mean loving less. It means loving without needing to own. You can cherish your children and still let them become who they are. You can enjoy your home and still not fall apart when the roof leaks. The calm in the ninth Guru's hymns isn't distance. It's the loose, open hand that lets love stay.
screen: `DETACHMENT ISN'T RUNNING AWAY.` · `THE GURU WAS A HOUSEHOLDER.` · `THE LOTUS IN WATER STAYS DRY.` · `THE OPEN HAND LETS LOVE STAY.` · then, large: `LOVE WITHOUT CLUTCHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love someone without clutching. Bring to mind someone you love deeply, and notice any place where love has turned into gripping: worry about their choices, a need for them to call, a fear of losing them. Don't scold yourself. Just open your hands in your lap, palms up, and breathe. Hold them in mind the way that parent's hand rests on the bike seat: there, but light. Wish them well, exactly as they are. If you pray, you can place them in Waheguru's care. The bell holds the time.
Kamal, lotus. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, detachment means love without clutching: living in the world like a kamal in water.
Your line: love without clutching. Today, with one person you love, loosen one grip: a check-in you don't need, a piece of advice you don't give. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: The Sikh path is a householder's path, with work and family, and Sikhs describe the Gurus' ideal as staying unattached in the world like a lotus in water; Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns are often sung as reminders of that steady, open love.

fork.setup: the hymns keep saying the world is passing. what does that mean for the people you love?
options: love them less, so it hurts less.
love them with an open hand, without clutching.
leave them and go to the forest.
fork.reveal: Sikh detachment isn't distance. like the lotus that grows in water but stays dry, it's love that holds without gripping.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kamal, lotus. Gurbani's picture of living in the world, in the water but not soaked.

trapdoor: what you thought: detachment means not caring.
what it means: it means loving without needing to own, steady when things pass.
what a scholar hears: the lotus and the waterbird come from Guru Nanak's Siddh Gosht, where he answers yogis who had left the world, so the image was made for exactly this question.
